vignette:
David, a 54-year-old civil servant, presents as a man worn thin by a vigilance he can no longer sustain. The events that brought him to therapy occurred eight months ago, but for David, the final night with his ex-partner, Mark, has never really ended. He speaks about it in a fragmented way, not because he is unwilling, but because he finds that when he tries to deliberately remember what happened, the memory itself feels inaccessible, like a locked room. The story, as he understands it, exists only in the intrusive flashes that ambush him during the day. He explains that remembering is not like watching a film, but like being shown a series of stark, silent photographs in his mind: Mark's face contorted with rage, the pattern of the wallpaper behind his head, a raised fist.

The final assault took place in their shared home, a culmination of months of escalating control and aggression. David was held down, his autonomy stripped away in a matter of moments. It is this feeling of absolute powerlessness that now haunts his daily life. At his job in a large municipal building, a surprise project reassignment or a last-minute change in deadlines can trigger a disproportionate sense of panic. The lack of control feels viscerally dangerous, echoing that night. This is especially potent when he is alone with male colleagues. A standard one-on-one meeting in his supervisor's small office becomes an ordeal; he feels the walls closing in, his breathing shallow, certain that he is trapped and something terrible is about to happen. He has started making excuses to keep the office door open or to have a third person present, a strategy that is becoming increasingly difficult to explain to his team.

When the photographic memories do break through, they bring with them a phantom taste. He can suddenly, vividly, taste the metallic tang of blood mixed with the stale whiskey on Mark's breath from that night. In those moments, he feels a profound sense of unreality, as if he is watching a scene that happened to someone else. He has learned to detach himself, to float away from the images and the taste, observing them from a great distance until they recede. This detachment is a shield, but it leaves him feeling hollowed out and disconnected from his own life.

After leaving Mark, David found a small apartment, but the silence and solitude he thought he craved quickly became terrifying. Being alone in a room, especially at night, felt like an invitation for danger. To combat this, he has systematically eliminated solitude from his life. His calendar is a frantic patchwork of social engagements and overtime at work. He keeps himself constantly surrounded by people, ensuring he is never alone with his thoughts. He hasn't spent a single night by himself since moving. He either stays on friends' couches or insists his new partner, Alan, stays with him. He knows this constant need for presence is a strain on their budding relationship. Sleeping in an unfamiliar place is equally impossible, making even a weekend trip to visit family a source of intense anxiety.

It is this exhaustion that has finally propelled him to seek help. The relentless effort of managing his world-of avoiding solitude, of navigating professional interactions that feel fraught with peril, of bracing against the next sensory snapshot-has depleted him. He came to therapy not with a dramatic story of a breakdown, but with a quiet admission of defeat. He is tired of being afraid in his own home. What frightens him most is the thought that this is permanent, that he will never again feel safe while alone. His hope is a simple one: to one day be able to close his own front door behind him and feel not terror, but peace.
